platforms.title: Tension Headache vs. Migraine: It's Not Just "a Bad Headache"
platforms.meta_description: Weekly headaches you've been blaming on stress could actually be migraine. How the American Migraine Foundation and ICHD-3 criteria tell the two apart.
platforms.body_html:
Getting a headache almost every week and chalking it up to stress? It might actually be migraine. The American Migraine Foundation explains that tension headache and migraine come from genuinely different mechanisms, not just different levels of the same pain. Treating every headache the same way with the same over-the-counter pill can mean missing the care that actually fits.

Why the pain feels so different

Tension headache shows up as a band-like pressure on both sides of the head, caused by sustained tightness in the neck, shoulder, and scalp muscles. Stress, poor posture, and long stretches staring at a screen are common triggers for that muscular tightening.

Migraine comes from an entirely different pathway. Under the International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD-3) criteria, overactive signaling between the trigeminal nerve and blood vessels in the brain produces a one-sided, throbbing pain that pulses in time with the heartbeat. Inflammatory substances released around those blood vessels during the process are part of why the pain quality feels so different from ordinary muscle soreness.

How to tell them apart, and what to watch for

First, whether nausea, vomiting, or sensitivity to light and sound show up. The American Migraine Foundation lists these as classic migraine companions. Tension headache rarely brings any of them along.

Second, whether ordinary movement, like climbing stairs, makes the pain noticeably worse. Migraine often flares up with routine physical activity, while tension headache usually doesn't care much either way. Some people also notice aura beforehand — zigzag light or flickering in their vision that signals a migraine is about to start.

What's worth being most careful about is reaching for over-the-counter painkillers more than 2 to 3 times a week out of habit. Doing so can trigger medication-overuse headache, where the pill itself becomes part of the reason headaches keep coming back more often. Simply raising the dose without figuring out which type of headache it is doesn't fix the underlying issue.

When it's hard to tell the two apart, it helps to jot down when the headache started, whether the pain sits on one side or both, any symptoms that came along with it, and exactly which painkiller was taken and how many times that day. That kind of log gives a doctor far more to work with than describing the pain from memory during a short visit. If headaches start showing up several times a month, or a headache suddenly feels different from the usual pattern — noticeably more intense, one-sided for the first time, or paired with new symptoms — it's safer to see a neurologist rather than guess at home. A headache diary kept for even two or three weeks often reveals a pattern that a single bad day never would, including which specific triggers, foods, or sleep changes tend to show up right before the worst episodes.

If your headaches are becoming more frequent or painkillers stop working as well as they used to, that's a clear sign to talk to a doctor rather than simply increasing the dose on your own.
